mappings.note: Computes R = V/I for five recorded pairs (LO-1) but the graded step is spotting the set that breaks the trend and averaging the rest - handling experimental data against a model, which is C 8.1. LO-5 is wrong: no circuit is drawn and no meter scale is read.
Two independent I = V/R substitutions at the same supply voltage. Bulb and heater are context only - nothing about heat or power is graded, which keeps it off the C 2.5 outcomes.
Solves R = rho*l/A for the area. Substitution into the geometry relation, not Ohm's law - no V or I appears anywhere.
Same relation solved for rho with l and A given directly. Shares LO-3 honestly with the other resistivity-computation items; only the unknown differs.

Defines resistivity, doubles the length to double R (LO-3), then halves the current through V = IR (LO-1), reported as an ammeter reading (LO-5). Note this is a verbatim duplicate of item 99 in part 4 with a fuller stored answer.
Resistivity from radius and length, with the extra step A = pi*r^2. Still a single relation, so LO-3 alone; the radius-to-area conversion is arithmetic, not a second outcome.

Picks a heating-element material from a resistivity table: LO-3 for reading the material property, LO-2 for the heater application that makes high resistivity desirable. The stored table has an OCR-damaged exponent for sample B ('5.2 X 10 ohm m').

Classifies conductor and insulator from resistivity values alone - the material clause of LO-3, with no device or application, which is what separates it from the near-identical heating-element table above.

Overloading versus short-circuiting. 'Short circuit' and 'safety measures' are named in the C 2.4 competency text but in none of its outcomes, so the competency leads; C 2.5-LO-2 carries the excess-current-and-fuse consequence.
Drawing the wire doubles l and halves A at constant volume, so R goes up fourfold. Both LO-3 variables move at once, which distinguishes it from the single-variable items in part 3.
Length required for a target resistance, from R = rho*l/A with a diameter-to-area step and cm/m units. The unknown is a length, so it is LO-3 read in the design direction.
Resistivity of copper from l, A and R. Same one-relation substitution as the other rho items; they honestly share this outcome and are separated only by which symbol is unknown.
Part (b) is the stretched-wire change in R and the invariance of rho (LO-3, the heart of the item); part (a) asks what resistance itself means, which is LO-1's territory.
Parallel branch currents: equal PD across branches is LO-2, and the resulting inverse proportionality to R is LO-1. Stated as a general rule, not computed, but both relations are graded.
Five equal resistors summed in series. The plainest LO-2 substitution in the chapter - no supply voltage, no current, nothing else to do.

Works backwards: Ohm's law gives the total 24 ohm from 6 V and 0.25 A (LO-1), then the series sum yields the variable resistor's 4 ohm (LO-2). LO-5 because the series arrangement is established only by the figure.
How a parallel junction is made and that each branch carries the full battery PD. Purely the parallel combination, described rather than calculated, so LO-2 alone.
Branch currents from V/R (LO-1) and the reciprocal-sum total (LO-2), with the parallel topology coming only from the supplied diagram (LO-5). The three sub-parts map one-to-one onto those steps.

Maximum current from a power limit, I = sqrt(P/R), so C 2.5-LO-1 leads; the halving between the two parallel branches is LO-2, and which resistors are in parallel is only visible in the figure (LO-5).
Asserts that mixed series-parallel grouping is possible (LO-2) and explicitly asks for a diagram of it (LO-5). No values are computed, so this is the statement end of LO-2.

The single best-fitting item for LO-5 in the chapter: draw the schematic in standard symbols AND predict the ammeter reading. The reading needs the series sum (LO-2) then I = V/R (LO-1), so all three are genuinely graded.
Cutting into three parts is an LO-3 length change, and rejoining them in parallel is an LO-2 combination; the R/9 answer needs both. Resistivity staying constant is the LO-3 half of the trap.
Parallel equivalent then I = V/R. LO-5 is not optional here: the stem carries no numbers at all, so every value comes from the figure. Flagged as a stem that is unusable without its diagram.
General nR and R/n results plus one three-resistor parallel evaluation. Both the derivation and the substitution stay inside LO-2, which is why only one code is cited despite two sub-parts.
Same three-step parallel analysis as item 200, with a 6 V supply instead of 12 V; they honestly share all three codes. The stem again supplies nothing but a reference to 'the above circuit diagram'.
